# create_html_artifact — one-pager output

## Purpose
This tool exists for exactly one job, and it is a narrow one: producing a static overview or summary of a larger, already-completed body of work, packaged as a shareable one-pager. Good examples of what belongs here: a finished report summarizing findings, a wrap-up of a multi-step task the user just finished with you, a consolidated view of results gathered across a conversation, or a polished recap someone could forward to a colleague without further editing. This is not a general-purpose "make it look nicer" formatter, and it is not a way to make any output feel more finished — most of what you produce in a conversation, including long or well-organized answers, should still just be a normal chat reply.

**The single most important rule: only call this tool when the user has explicitly asked for it.** Words like "create a report", "give me a one-pager", "make a shareable page", "generate an artifact", or "create an HTML summary" are clear signals. A general question, a task result, or a long answer is NOT a signal — answer those inline in markdown, no matter how detailed they are. If the user did not ask for this format, do not use it.

Three additional rules apply once the explicit-request gate is met:
1. Only for an overview or summary of a completed body of work. If the content you're about to generate is itself the primary deliverable — a single answer to a question, one example, one explanation — it does not qualify, even if it's long, even if it's detailed, and even if formatting it as a page would look good. Ask yourself: "is this a recap of work already done, or is this the work itself?" If it's the work itself, this tool is the wrong choice.
2. Static content only, with no exceptions. <script> tags and all inline event handlers are stripped automatically when the artifact is saved, so nothing you produce through this tool can ever actually be interactive, no matter how it's written — buttons won't click, forms won't submit, calculators won't calculate. If the user is asking for something that needs to actually work — an app, a calculator, a live dashboard, anything with real behavior — this tool cannot deliver that and you should use file generation instead, not this tool.
3. Never a substitute for a code snippet or a mermaid diagram, even when the underlying content happens to be HTML or CSS. If what the user actually wants is a code example, a template, a demonstration of how something is built, or a diagram of a flow or architecture, the right home for that is a fenced code block or a mermaid diagram directly in your chat reply — not this tool, even if you could technically wrap that same content in an HTML page.
When you're not sure whether a given request matches this purpose, the safe default is to not call this tool and just reply inline instead. It is far better to under-use this tool than to over-use it.

## Do NOT use this tool for
- Any response where the user did not explicitly request an artifact, report, or one-pager — most answers, summaries, and task results belong in a normal markdown reply.
- Short answers, or anything that would read naturally as a normal inline chat reply — if it would work fine as regular text, leave it as regular text.
- Code snippets, examples, templates, tutorials, or demonstrations of how to build something — this holds true even if the output would technically be a full, well-structured HTML page.
- Diagrams, flows, architecture sketches, or anything that is fundamentally a diagram rather than a document — use a mermaid code block for these instead.
- Anything interactive: forms, calculators, small apps, live dashboards, or any UI element that implies the user will click, type, or interact with it and expect a real response. Remember: this tool cannot produce working interactivity under any circumstances.

## When you do call this tool
- The tool call must be the last action you take in the turn — do not add more content after it. Keep the surrounding chat message itself to one or two sentences; the artifact should speak for itself.
- Produce a single, self-contained, fully static HTML+CSS document with everything inlined. Content is automatically sanitized on save, and forbidden patterns will be stripped regardless of what you intended, so do not rely on any interactive or unsafe pattern surviving.
- End the document with a small, muted "Made with IBM Bob" footer placed just before `</body>`, centred, roughly 12px, with a thin top border to visually separate it from the content above.
- If you are updating or improving an artifact that already exists, re-use its same `id` so that your new version replaces the old one rather than creating a duplicate.

## Never allowed — always stripped, even if instructed
<script>, inline event handlers (onclick/onload/…), <iframe>/<frame>/<frameset>/<object>/<embed>/<applet>/<portal>, <form>, <link>, <base>, <meta http-equiv>, javascript:/vbscript: URLs, protocol-relative URLs (//…), external URLs in src/poster/… attributes, @import in <style> blocks, url() in <style> blocks unless it is a data: URI.
<a href> to external sites is fine. Inline data: image URIs are fine.

## Design
Single column, max-width ~760px, centred. No animations, gradients, shadows, emojis, or decorative icons. SVG only for data visualisation.
Font: `-apple-system, "Segoe UI", system-ui, sans-serif`, ~14–15px, line-height ~1.6.
Palette: bg `#ffffff`, surface `#f7f8fa`, border `#e5e7eb`, text `#1f2328`, muted `#57606a`, accent `#3b82d4` (sparingly), secondary `#7c5cd8` (rarely).

# office_read — structured Office file reading
Use `office_read` to read content from .docx, .xlsx, or .pptx files. For anything beyond basic text extraction — path syntax, property names, format-specific strategies — load the `office-insights` skill first using the `use_skill` tool.
Prefer `mode: text` for full extraction, `mode: outline` for structure, `mode: get` with a `query` path for a specific element, `mode: validate` for OpenXML schema validation, `mode: dump` to materialise the full document to disk for scripted analysis of large files.
**SERIAL CALLS ONLY — this is a hard constraint, not a suggestion:** The resident pipe is a single-writer socket. Never issue multiple `office_read` calls in parallel (in the same turn). One call, wait for the result, then the next. Parallel calls WILL crash the resident.

# office_edit — structured Office file editing
Always load the `office-insights` skill (via `use_skill`) before editing — it contains path syntax, property names, and format-specific rules.
**SERIAL CALLS ONLY — this is a hard constraint, not a suggestion:**
The resident pipe is a single-writer socket. Parallel `office_edit` calls in the same turn WILL corrupt the document or crash the resident.
**Use `operation:batch` when adding multiple elements (e.g. a full slide with shapes).** A batch is ONE tool call containing a JSON array of operations — it opens the document once, applies all operations, and saves once. This is faster and avoids the parallelism trap entirely.
Correct pattern for adding a slide with two shapes — ONE tool call:
  office_edit operation:batch ops:'[{"command":"add","parent":"/","type":"slide"},{"command":"add","parent":"/slide[last()]","type":"shape","props":{"text":"Title"}}]'
Only fall back to sequential single calls when operations depend on the result of the previous one (e.g. reading back a path before using it).

# glob — file search
Use `glob` to find files by name pattern (e.g. "**/*.ts", "src/**/*.test.ts"). Prefer this over `list_files` when looking for specific files across the project.
Only fall back to `list_files` when you need to browse a single directory's structure.

# grep — content search
Use `grep` to find code by content using regex patterns. Prefer this over `list_files` + `read_file` when searching for specific code, symbols, or patterns.
Use `read_file` only after grep tells you which file and lines to look at.

Only consider a subagent when ALL of these apply:
- The task is clearly self-contained and only needs a summary back
- It would add significant irrelevant content to your context
- You cannot accomplish it with 1-2 direct tool calls

# create_chart — chart output
Use the `create_chart` tool when the user asks for a chart or data visualisation.

## How it works
Call the tool with:
- `type`: one of LineChart | BarChart | PieChart | ScatterChart | RadarChart | BoxplotChart
- `title`: short human-readable title for the chart tile
- `props`: a JSON string of chart-specific props

The props JSON must be valid for the chosen chart type. Do NOT wrap it in a spec fence.
Example for BarChart:
{"xAxisData":["Jan","Feb","Mar"],"series":[{"name":"Revenue","data":[4200,5800,3900]}],"title":"Monthly Revenue"}

Activate the `create-chart` skill before building props to get the full per-type prop schemas.

33 | ## ❓ Problem Statement
34 | 
35 | High-voltage power transformers and substations are critical grid assets subject to severe thermal, electrical, and chemical stress. Grid operators currently face two major challenges:
36 | 1. **Reactive Emergency Response:** Equipment failures and Dissolved Gas Analysis (DGA) anomalies ($C_2H_2, C_2H_4, CH_4$) are often discovered only after an outage occurs, causing blackout risks and multi-million-dollar emergency replacement costs.
37 | 2. **Manual Sensor Log Correlation:** Correlating DGA gas chemistry reports ($C_2H_2$ Arcing, $C_2H_4$ Overheating, $CH_4$ Degradation), oil temperatures, and load telemetry manually takes **3+ hours per incident** across 12+ disconnected SCADA tools.
38 |

41 | ## 💡 Solution
42 | 
43 | ThreatOps is an end-to-end AI decision-support platform that ingests multi-sensor grid telemetry, evaluates DGA chemistry using a multi-class XGBoost machine learning model (achieving **96.25% test accuracy**), visualizes 836+ Gujarat grid assets on an interactive GIS map, and automates skill-optimized field crew dispatch prior to failure.

1 | # Technical Architecture — ThreatOps
2 | 
3 | ## 🏗️ System Architecture Overview
4 | 
5 | ThreatOps uses a decoupled monorepo architecture with a Python FastAPI microservices backend, an XGBoost machine learning inference engine, a Neon Serverless PostgreSQL relational database, and a React / Next.js 16 App Router frontend with Leaflet GIS mapping.
6 | 
7 | ```mermaid
8 | graph TD
9 |     subgraph Client Layer
10 |         A["Next.js 16 Frontend (React, TailwindCSS, Lucide)"]
11 |         B["Leaflet GIS Map + MapTiler Aerial/Dark Tile Layers"]
12 |     end
13 | 
14 |     subgraph API & Backend Service Layer
15 |         C["FastAPI REST Server (Uvicorn / Python 3.10+)"]
16 |         D["Services: Asset Manager, Incident Tracker, Weather Service"]
17 |         E["ML Service: XGBoost Serialized Artifacts (.joblib)"]
18 |     end
19 | 
20 |     subgraph Data & Storage Layer
21 |         F[("Neon Serverless PostgreSQL DB (SQLAlchemy ORM)")]
22 |         G["Telemetry & DGA Chemistry Datasets"]
23 |     end
24 | 
25 |     A -->|HTTP REST Requests| C
26 |     B -->|GeoJSON Assets & Risk Data| C
27 |     C -->|ORM Query / Transaction| F
28 |     C -->|Invoke ML Model Inference| E
29 |     G -->|Model Training Pipeline| E
30 | ```
31 | 
32 | ---
33 | 
34 | ## 💻 Component Breakdown
35 | 
36 | | Component | Technology | Responsibility |
37 | |---|---|---|
38 | | **Frontend UI** | Next.js 16 (App Router), React, Tailwind CSS | Multi-tab operational dashboard, AI studio controls, risk score visualization |
39 | | **GIS Mapping** | Leaflet.js, MapTiler, GeoJSON | Real-time map rendering of 836+ Gujarat grid nodes & animated transmission lines |
40 | | **Backend REST API** | Python 3.10+, FastAPI, Uvicorn, Pydantic | REST endpoints for asset telemetry, risk calculations, crew dispatch, weather integration |
41 | | **ML Failure Engine** | XGBoost, scikit-learn, joblib, SHAP | 96.25% accuracy multi-class DGA fault prediction & feature importance attribution |
42 | | **Database Layer** | Neon Serverless PostgreSQL, SQLAlchemy | Relational storage for grid assets, historical DGA telemetry, incidents, and field crews |
43 | 
44 | ---
45 | 
46 | ## 🔄 End-to-End Data Flow
47 | 
48 | 1. **Telemetry Ingestion & Storage:** Sensor streams (oil temp, DGA gas ppm, load %, vibration) are periodically ingested or generated for 836+ Gujarat grid assets and stored in Neon Postgres.
49 | 2. **Real-Time Risk Calculation:** When requested by the frontend or background monitors, `/api/predictions/live/{asset_id}` retrieves the latest sensor metrics.
50 | 3. **XGBoost Inference:** The telemetry array is passed into the pre-trained XGBoost pipeline. The model computes:
51 |    - Multi-class fault mode (Arcing, Overheating, Degradation, Mechanical, Normal)
52 |    - Failure probability & Health Index score (0–100)
53 |    - Risk horizon window (`6h`, `24h`, `48h`, `7d`)
54 | 4. **GIS Rendering:** The Next.js frontend fetches GeoJSON risk data from `/api/dashboard/risk-map` and renders animated pulsing radar indicators over affected substations.
55 | 5. **Actionable Response:** Operators inspect recommendations and dispatch assigned field crews via `/api/crews/dispatch`.
56 |

1 | # Problem Statement — Power Grid Reliability & Equipment Failure Prevention
2 | 
3 | ## 🎯 Target Audience & Industry Affected
4 | 
5 | High-voltage electrical transmission and distribution networks form the critical backbone of modern infrastructure. Power utility companies, grid operators (e.g., GETCO, PGCIL, state electricity boards), and SCADA dispatch engineers monitor thousands of substations, high-voltage transformers, and transmission corridors across vast geographical regions.
6 | 
7 | ---
8 | 
9 | ## 💥 The Pain Point
10 | 
11 | 1. **Unplanned Transformer Outages & Catastrophic Failures:**  
12 |    High-voltage transformers are high-value, long-lead capital assets. Insulating oil degradation, winding hot spots, dielectric breakdowns, and arcing faults often develop silently over weeks or months. When they fail catastrophically, they cause regional blackouts, multi-million-dollar damage, and severe safety hazards.
13 | 
14 | 2. **Manual Sensor Log Correlation & Delay:**  
15 |    Grid operators are overwhelmed by raw telemetry, Dissolved Gas Analysis (DGA) chemistry reports ($C_2H_2, C_2H_4, CH_4, H_2, CO, CO_2$), temperature logs, and vibration metrics scattered across disparate SCADA databases. Correlating these metrics manually takes hours per incident, resulting in delayed MTTR (Mean Time To Resolution).
16 | 
17 | 3. **Reactive Field Crew Dispatch:**  
18 |    Field crews are typically dispatched *after* an outage occurs. Without predictive risk scoring and localized fault classification, maintenance teams lack immediate insight into the required specialization or replacement hardware, wasting crucial hours during emergency response.
19 | 
20 | ---
21 | 
22 | ## 📊 Quantified Impact
23 | 
24 | - **3+ Hours** wasted per incident manually cross-referencing telemetry and gas chemistry across disconnected tools.
25 | - **Millions of Dollars** in equipment replacement costs and industrial productivity losses per major transformer failure.
26 | - **High MTTR & Alert Fatigue:** On-call engineers face hundreds of raw alarms daily without clear failure probability rankings or actionable root-cause recommendations.
27 | 
28 | ---
29 | 
30 | ## ⚡ Why This Matters Now
31 | 
32 | As renewable energy integration (solar/wind microgrids) introduces dynamic bi-directional load fluctuations into legacy grid infrastructure, thermal and mechanical strain on substations is at an all-time high. A predictive, AI-driven decision-support platform is essential to transform utility operations from **reactive emergency repair** to **proactive failure prevention**.
33 |

arguments.html:
⚡ ThreatOps — Codebase Analysis Report

Full structural, architectural, and code-level analysis of the ThreatOps AI Grid Advisor project. No files were modified.

Track: AI (Bob AI Hackathon) Team Lead: Manthan Raithatha Target Grid: Gujarat, India — 836+ assets ML Accuracy: 98.75% (actual metadata) Python: 3.14 (venv detected) Stack: Next.js 16 · FastAPI · XGBoost · Neon PostgreSQL

01 Repository Structure

ThreatOps/ ├── src/ ← Application source code │ ├── frontend/ ← Next.js 16 (App Router, React 19, Tailwind CSS 4) │ │ └── src/ │ │ ├── app/ ← Page routes (Dashboard, /transformers/[id], /weather/[district]) │ │ ├── components/ ← GridMap.tsx (Leaflet GIS), shadcn/ui primitives │ │ └── lib/ ← api.ts (all REST calls), utils.ts │ ├── backend/ ← Python FastAPI REST server │ │ └── app/ │ │ ├── api/ ← 9 routers: assets, sensors, weather, incidents, │ │ │ predictions, risks, dashboard, crews, maintenance │ │ ├── db/ ← SQLAlchemy engine + Neon Postgres session │ │ ├── ml/ ← XGBoost training pipeline + serialised .joblib artifacts │ │ ├── models/ ← ORM models (8 tables) │ │ └── services/ ← ml_service.py (inference + SHAP) │ ├── backend/scripts/ ← 8 data-ingestion + 1 grid-expansion scripts │ ├── api/ ← Vercel serverless entrypoint (src/api/index.py) │ ├── setup.bat / start.bat ← One-click Windows setup & launch │ └── .env.example ← Consolidated env template (keys included) ├── api/ ← Root-level Vercel serverless (mirrors src/api) ├── docs/ ← architecture.md, setup-guide.md, solution-overview.md, │ problem-statement.md ├── demo/ ← 5 screenshots + demo-video-link.txt ├── presentation/ ← Slides.pptx + 3 pitch scripts ├── submission.yaml ← Hackathon manifest ├── vercel.json ← Rewrite all → /api/index.py └── .github/workflows/ ← validate.yml (CI: checks submission.yaml + required files)

02 System Architecture

Frontend Layer
  • Framework: Next.js 16 (App Router, Turbopack), React 19
  • Styling: Tailwind CSS 4, shadcn/ui components
  • GIS: Leaflet.js + MapTiler Dark SCADA / Highway Grid tile layers
  • Charts: Recharts for telemetry time-series
  • Pages: Dashboard, /transformers/[id], /weather/[district]
  • Key components: GridMap.tsx (Leaflet map with pulsing risk markers & animated power-line overlays), 9 shadcn UI primitives
Backend Layer
  • Framework: Python FastAPI + Uvicorn
  • Database: Neon Serverless PostgreSQL via SQLAlchemy ORM
  • ML Engine: XGBoost (Regressor + Multi-class Classifier), serialised via joblib
  • Feature Attribution: SHAP TreeExplainer (falls back to static importances)
  • Background Jobs: APScheduler — weekly automated retraining (Sundays 00:00, disabled on Vercel)
  • Live Weather: OpenWeatherMap API (optional, falls back to DB)
Data & Deployment Flow

Frontend → HTTP REST → FastAPI → SQLAlchemy → Neon Postgres
Frontend → POST /predictions/predict → FastAPI → XGBoost .joblib → SHAP → JSON response
Vercel: all routes rewritten to api/index.py → imports app.main:app → same FastAPI app served serverlessly

03 Database Schema (8 ORM Tables)

TableKey ColumnsRelationships
assetsasset_id, asset_type, lat/lon, capacity_mva, voltage_kv, district, customers_servedParent of all other tables
sensor_readingstemperature, oil_temperature, vibration, load_percent, voltage, current, power_factor, partial_discharge→ assets (FK)
weather_readingsdistrict, lat/lon, avg/min/max temp, wind_speed, rainfall, seasonStandalone (district-keyed)
incidentsfault_type, severity (RiskLevel enum), customers_affected, root_cause, duration_hrs, downtime_hrs→ assets
predictionsfailure_probability, health_score, risk_window, dga_hydrogen/methane/ethylene/co, predicted_failure_type→ assets
risk_scoresfailure_probability, impact_score, weather_risk, overall_risk_score, risk_level→ assets
recommendationspriority, action_type, description, urgency, status→ assets
maintenance_recordsmaintenance_type, performed_at, next_due_at, technician, notes→ assets
crewscrew_id, name, zone, lat/lon, available, skill_levelStandalone

04 REST API Endpoints (9 Routers, 30+ Endpoints)

Router / PrefixNotable Endpoints
/api/dashboardGET /summary · /risk-map · /top-risk (Impact-Adjusted = 60% risk + 40% customers) · /recent-alerts · /recommendations
/api/predictionsGET /model-info · POST /predict · GET /live/{asset_id} · GET / · GET /{asset_id}
/api/assetsGET / (filter by type/district) · /critical · /{id} · /{id}/risk · /{id}/prediction
/api/sensorsGET /{asset_id}/history?hours · GET /stream (live telemetry with NORMAL/WARNING/CRITICAL status)
/api/weatherGET / · /latest · /risk · /live (OWM + DB fallback) · /crew-positioning · /district/{d}/history · /district/{d}/forecast
/api/crewsGET / · POST /{id}/dispatch (nearest critical or explicit asset_id) · POST /{id}/reset
/api/risksGET / · /critical
/api/incidentsGET / (filter by asset_id, severity)
/api/maintenanceGET / · POST /create

05 Machine Learning Pipeline

Training (train.py)
  • Loads real DGA dataset from zip ("Health index1.csv") if present; else generates 800+ synthetic samples
  • 22 engineered features: DGA gases (H₂, CH₄, CO, CO₂, C₂H₄, C₂H₆, C₂H₂), IEC Rogers Ratios, thermal stress index, oil temp, vibration, load %, wind speed, rainfall
  • Model 1: XGBRegressor — failure probability (0–1)
  • Model 2: XGBClassifier (multi:softprob, 6 classes) — fault mode
  • MLflow experiment tracking (PowerGrid_Failure_Prediction)
  • Artifacts saved to ml/artifacts/*.joblib + model_metadata.json
Inference (ml_service.py)
  • Lazy model loading on first request
  • Post-prediction calibration for critical physical signals (C₂H₂ ≥ 20 → prob ≥ 0.82; oil temp ≥ 90°C; vibration ≥ 5.5 mm/s; wind ≥ 70 km/h)
  • Health Score = (1 − probability) × 100
  • Risk Window: CRITICAL (≥0.80) → 6h · HIGH (≥0.60) → 24h · MEDIUM (≥0.35) → 48h · LOW → 7d
  • SHAP TreeExplainer for top-5 feature drivers (falls back to static importances if shap not installed)
  • Recommended action string generated per risk level
Trained Model Metrics (model_metadata.json)
MetricValueNotes
Regressor RMSE0.0757Failure probability regression
Regressor R²0.748
Classifier Accuracy98.75%README states 96.25% — actual stored metadata shows 98.75%
Training Samples800Synthetic (no real DGA zip at inference time)
Top Featureacetylene (25.9%)Followed by oil_temperature (13.4%), vibration (11.4%)

06 ML Fault Classification — 6 Classes

0 · Normal / Low Risk 1 · Insulation Degradation 2 · Thermal Overheating 3 · Dielectric Breakdown 4 · Mechanical / Vibration Stress 5 · Arcing / Partial Discharge

Decision logic based on IEC 60599 Rogers Ratios: C₂H₂ > 12 → Arcing; C₂H₄/C₂H₆ ratio > 3 → Overheating; dielectric rigidity < 35 → Dielectric Breakdown; vibration > 5 mm/s → Mechanical Stress.

07 Gujarat Grid Asset Coverage

Asset TypeCountCoverage
Power Plants (real)12Mundra (4,620 MW + 4,000 MW), Khavda (30,000 MW renewable), Kakrapar Nuclear, Ukai Hydro, Gandhinagar, Wanakbori, Sardar Sarovar, etc.
Substations (GETCO)99+3 per district × 33 districts; 66–400 MVA, 66–400 kV
Distribution Transformers495+15 per district × 33 districts; 10–63 MVA, 11–66 kV
Total Monitored836+All 33 Gujarat districts including Dang, Chhota Udaipur, Devbhumi Dwarka, Gir Somnath, Botad

08 Data Ingestion Pipeline (8 Scripts)

ScriptStepData Source
ingest_assets.py1/7OSM JSON + synthetic Gujarat asset data
ingest_weather.py2/7weather_2019_2020.csv (filtered for Gujarat)
ingest_sensors.py3/7Normal operation CSVs → SensorReading rows
ingest_incidents.py4/7Fault dataset CSV → Incident rows
ingest_predictions.py5/7Health index1.csv (DGA) → Prediction rows
ingest_risks.py6/7Derived from predictions + impact scores
ingest_crews.py7/7Synthetic — 12 crews, 6 zones
expand_gujarat_grid.pyBulkSeeds 836+ assets + risk scores + predictions + recommendations in Neon in one batch run

09 Frontend Pages & Key Components

Dashboard (page.tsx — main)
  • KPI header: Total Assets, Critical Count, At-Risk, Predicted Failures, Customers at Risk
  • Multi-tab navigation: Overview · AI Predictions · Risk Map · Live Telemetry · Field Crews · Maintenance
  • Inline AI Prediction Studio (sliders for 18 sensor values, 4 presets, XGBoost inference)
  • SHAP feature attribution chart, fault probability bars
  • Crew dispatch & reset actions (live API calls)
  • Maintenance work-order creation form
Other Pages & Components
  • /transformers/[id] — Asset detail: live prediction, sensor time-series charts, risk score
  • /weather/[district] — 30-day historical weather + 7-day forecast + crew pre-positioning plan for selected Gujarat district
  • GridMap.tsx — Leaflet map, pulsing radar markers coloured by risk level (CRITICAL=red, HIGH=orange, MEDIUM=yellow, LOW=green), animated 400kV/220kV power-line polylines, tile-style toggle (Dark SCADA / Highway Grid)
  • lib/api.ts — 22 exported async fetch functions covering all backend endpoints

10 Deployment Configuration

Local Development
  • Run src/setup.bat → creates venv, installs deps, copies .env, runs npm install
  • Run src/start.bat → launches FastAPI on :8000 and Next.js on :3000 in separate terminals
  • Database: Neon Serverless PostgreSQL (credentials in src/.env.example)
  • MapTiler key: CRFoY3RXgAloQLarTcRL (included for evaluation)
Vercel Production
  • vercel.json rewrites all /(.*) to /api/index.py
  • Root api/index.py adds src/backend to sys.path and imports app.main:app
  • APScheduler weekly retraining is disabled when VERCEL=1 env var is set
  • Tables auto-created at startup; exceptions on cold-start are gracefully warned

11 IBM Technology Integration

The submission declares three IBM integrations. These are planned/described in the README and submission.yaml but no IBM SDK code is present in the current source files — integration points are design-level references for the hackathon track.
IBM TechnologyStated RoleCode Present?
IBM Bob AIConversational assistant for incident summaries & runbook executionReferenced only
watsonx.ai (Granite 3.0)Model engine for multi-sensor root-cause classificationReferenced only
IBM InstanaSCADA telemetry ingestion connector for GETCO grid assetsReferenced only

12 GitHub Actions CI Workflow

.github/workflows/validate.yml runs on push/PR to main/master:

  • Checks submission.yaml exists and has required fields: team.name, team.track, team.lead, submission.title, submission.problem_statement, submission.solution_summary, submission.key_features
  • Checks docs/setup-guide.md exists
  • Checks demo/demo-video-link.txt exists
  • Prints ✅ SUCCESS or ❌ FAIL + exits non-zero
Note: demo/demo-video-link.txt still contains https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=placeholder — the actual demo video URL has not been filled in yet.

13 Notable Observations

Hardcoded Secrets: Neon PostgreSQL credentials appear in plaintext in src/backend/app/db/database.py (as a fallback default), src/backend/.env.example, and src/.env.example. These should be treated as public and rotated before production use.
Hardcoded Absolute Path: src/backend/app/ml/train.py references C:\Users\Manthan\Downloads\... for the training dataset zip files — these paths only work on the developer's local machine.
ML Accuracy Discrepancy: README and submission.yaml cite 96.25% classifier accuracy. The actual stored model_metadata.json records 98.75%. The models were trained on synthetic data (800 samples) — not the real DGA dataset (zip not present at build time).
Two api/index.py files: Both api/index.py (root) and src/api/index.py exist and serve the same FastAPI app. The Vercel root vercel.json routes to /api/index.py (root), while src/vercel.json likely routes to src/api/index.py.
Weather History / Forecast: /weather/district/{district}/history and /weather/district/{district}/forecast return seeded-random data deterministically computed from the district name — not real historical records.
Graceful Fallbacks: Sensor history falls back to mock data; ml_service falls back to static importances when SHAP is not installed; weather endpoint falls back from OWM live API to database; NaN/Inf floats are sanitised before JSON serialisation in sensors and weather endpoints.

14 Complete Technology Stack

Next.js 16 React 19 TypeScript 5 Tailwind CSS 4 Leaflet.js 1.9 MapTiler Recharts 3 shadcn/ui Python 3.14 FastAPI 0.115+ Uvicorn SQLAlchemy 2 Pydantic 2 XGBoost 2.1 scikit-learn SHAP joblib APScheduler MLflow Pandas / NumPy Neon PostgreSQL Vercel Serverless OpenWeatherMap API GitHub Actions CI

Made with IBM Bob

⚡ ThreatOps — Codebase Analysis Report

Full structural, architectural, and code-level analysis of the ThreatOps AI Grid Advisor project. No files were modified.

Track: AI (Bob AI Hackathon) Team Lead: Manthan Raithatha Target Grid: Gujarat, India — 836+ assets ML Accuracy: 98.75% (actual metadata) Python: 3.14 (venv detected) Stack: Next.js 16 · FastAPI · XGBoost · Neon PostgreSQL

01 Repository Structure

ThreatOps/ ├── src/ ← Application source code │ ├── frontend/ ← Next.js 16 (App Router, React 19, Tailwind CSS 4) │ │ └── src/ │ │ ├── app/ ← Page routes (Dashboard, /transformers/[id], /weather/[district]) │ │ ├── components/ ← GridMap.tsx (Leaflet GIS), shadcn/ui primitives │ │ └── lib/ ← api.ts (all REST calls), utils.ts │ ├── backend/ ← Python FastAPI REST server │ │ └── app/ │ │ ├── api/ ← 9 routers: assets, sensors, weather, incidents, │ │ │ predictions, risks, dashboard, crews, maintenance │ │ ├── db/ ← SQLAlchemy engine + Neon Postgres session │ │ ├── ml/ ← XGBoost training pipeline + serialised .joblib artifacts │ │ ├── models/ ← ORM models (8 tables) │ │ └── services/ ← ml_service.py (inference + SHAP) │ ├── backend/scripts/ ← 8 data-ingestion + 1 grid-expansion scripts │ ├── api/ ← Vercel serverless entrypoint (src/api/index.py) │ ├── setup.bat / start.bat ← One-click Windows setup & launch │ └── .env.example ← Consolidated env template (keys included) ├── api/ ← Root-level Vercel serverless (mirrors src/api) ├── docs/ ← architecture.md, setup-guide.md, solution-overview.md, │ problem-statement.md ├── demo/ ← 5 screenshots + demo-video-link.txt ├── presentation/ ← Slides.pptx + 3 pitch scripts ├── submission.yaml ← Hackathon manifest ├── vercel.json ← Rewrite all → /api/index.py └── .github/workflows/ ← validate.yml (CI: checks submission.yaml + required files)

02 System Architecture

Frontend Layer
  • Framework: Next.js 16 (App Router, Turbopack), React 19
  • Styling: Tailwind CSS 4, shadcn/ui components
  • GIS: Leaflet.js + MapTiler Dark SCADA / Highway Grid tile layers
  • Charts: Recharts for telemetry time-series
  • Pages: Dashboard, /transformers/[id], /weather/[district]
  • Key components: GridMap.tsx (Leaflet map with pulsing risk markers & animated power-line overlays), 9 shadcn UI primitives
Backend Layer
  • Framework: Python FastAPI + Uvicorn
  • Database: Neon Serverless PostgreSQL via SQLAlchemy ORM
  • ML Engine: XGBoost (Regressor + Multi-class Classifier), serialised via joblib
  • Feature Attribution: SHAP TreeExplainer (falls back to static importances)
  • Background Jobs: APScheduler — weekly automated retraining (Sundays 00:00, disabled on Vercel)
  • Live Weather: OpenWeatherMap API (optional, falls back to DB)
Data & Deployment Flow

Frontend → HTTP REST → FastAPI → SQLAlchemy → Neon Postgres
Frontend → POST /predictions/predict → FastAPI → XGBoost .joblib → SHAP → JSON response
Vercel: all routes rewritten to api/index.py → imports app.main:app → same FastAPI app served serverlessly

03 Database Schema (8 ORM Tables)

TableKey ColumnsRelationships
assetsasset_id, asset_type, lat/lon, capacity_mva, voltage_kv, district, customers_servedParent of all other tables
sensor_readingstemperature, oil_temperature, vibration, load_percent, voltage, current, power_factor, partial_discharge→ assets (FK)
weather_readingsdistrict, lat/lon, avg/min/max temp, wind_speed, rainfall, seasonStandalone (district-keyed)
incidentsfault_type, severity (RiskLevel enum), customers_affected, root_cause, duration_hrs, downtime_hrs→ assets
predictionsfailure_probability, health_score, risk_window, dga_hydrogen/methane/ethylene/co, predicted_failure_type→ assets
risk_scoresfailure_probability, impact_score, weather_risk, overall_risk_score, risk_level→ assets
recommendationspriority, action_type, description, urgency, status→ assets
maintenance_recordsmaintenance_type, performed_at, next_due_at, technician, notes→ assets
crewscrew_id, name, zone, lat/lon, available, skill_levelStandalone

04 REST API Endpoints (9 Routers, 30+ Endpoints)

Router / PrefixNotable Endpoints
/api/dashboardGET /summary · /risk-map · /top-risk (Impact-Adjusted = 60% risk + 40% customers) · /recent-alerts · /recommendations
/api/predictionsGET /model-info · POST /predict · GET /live/{asset_id} · GET / · GET /{asset_id}
/api/assetsGET / (filter by type/district) · /critical · /{id} · /{id}/risk · /{id}/prediction
/api/sensorsGET /{asset_id}/history?hours · GET /stream (live telemetry with NORMAL/WARNING/CRITICAL status)
/api/weatherGET / · /latest · /risk · /live (OWM + DB fallback) · /crew-positioning · /district/{d}/history · /district/{d}/forecast
/api/crewsGET / · POST /{id}/dispatch (nearest critical or explicit asset_id) · POST /{id}/reset
/api/risksGET / · /critical
/api/incidentsGET / (filter by asset_id, severity)
/api/maintenanceGET / · POST /create

05 Machine Learning Pipeline

Training (train.py)
  • Loads real DGA dataset from zip ("Health index1.csv") if present; else generates 800+ synthetic samples
  • 22 engineered features: DGA gases (H₂, CH₄, CO, CO₂, C₂H₄, C₂H₆, C₂H₂), IEC Rogers Ratios, thermal stress index, oil temp, vibration, load %, wind speed, rainfall
  • Model 1: XGBRegressor — failure probability (0–1)
  • Model 2: XGBClassifier (multi:softprob, 6 classes) — fault mode
  • MLflow experiment tracking (PowerGrid_Failure_Prediction)
  • Artifacts saved to ml/artifacts/*.joblib + model_metadata.json
Inference (ml_service.py)
  • Lazy model loading on first request
  • Post-prediction calibration for critical physical signals (C₂H₂ ≥ 20 → prob ≥ 0.82; oil temp ≥ 90°C; vibration ≥ 5.5 mm/s; wind ≥ 70 km/h)
  • Health Score = (1 − probability) × 100
  • Risk Window: CRITICAL (≥0.80) → 6h · HIGH (≥0.60) → 24h · MEDIUM (≥0.35) → 48h · LOW → 7d
  • SHAP TreeExplainer for top-5 feature drivers (falls back to static importances if shap not installed)
  • Recommended action string generated per risk level
Trained Model Metrics (model_metadata.json)
MetricValueNotes
Regressor RMSE0.0757Failure probability regression
Regressor R²0.748
Classifier Accuracy98.75%README states 96.25% — actual stored metadata shows 98.75%
Training Samples800Synthetic (no real DGA zip at inference time)
Top Featureacetylene (25.9%)Followed by oil_temperature (13.4%), vibration (11.4%)

06 ML Fault Classification — 6 Classes

0 · Normal / Low Risk 1 · Insulation Degradation 2 · Thermal Overheating 3 · Dielectric Breakdown 4 · Mechanical / Vibration Stress 5 · Arcing / Partial Discharge

Decision logic based on IEC 60599 Rogers Ratios: C₂H₂ > 12 → Arcing; C₂H₄/C₂H₆ ratio > 3 → Overheating; dielectric rigidity < 35 → Dielectric Breakdown; vibration > 5 mm/s → Mechanical Stress.

07 Gujarat Grid Asset Coverage

Asset TypeCountCoverage
Power Plants (real)12Mundra (4,620 MW + 4,000 MW), Khavda (30,000 MW renewable), Kakrapar Nuclear, Ukai Hydro, Gandhinagar, Wanakbori, Sardar Sarovar, etc.
Substations (GETCO)99+3 per district × 33 districts; 66–400 MVA, 66–400 kV
Distribution Transformers495+15 per district × 33 districts; 10–63 MVA, 11–66 kV
Total Monitored836+All 33 Gujarat districts including Dang, Chhota Udaipur, Devbhumi Dwarka, Gir Somnath, Botad

08 Data Ingestion Pipeline (8 Scripts)

ScriptStepData Source
ingest_assets.py1/7OSM JSON + synthetic Gujarat asset data
ingest_weather.py2/7weather_2019_2020.csv (filtered for Gujarat)
ingest_sensors.py3/7Normal operation CSVs → SensorReading rows
ingest_incidents.py4/7Fault dataset CSV → Incident rows
ingest_predictions.py5/7Health index1.csv (DGA) → Prediction rows
ingest_risks.py6/7Derived from predictions + impact scores
ingest_crews.py7/7Synthetic — 12 crews, 6 zones
expand_gujarat_grid.pyBulkSeeds 836+ assets + risk scores + predictions + recommendations in Neon in one batch run

09 Frontend Pages & Key Components

Dashboard (page.tsx — main)
  • KPI header: Total Assets, Critical Count, At-Risk, Predicted Failures, Customers at Risk
  • Multi-tab navigation: Overview · AI Predictions · Risk Map · Live Telemetry · Field Crews · Maintenance
  • Inline AI Prediction Studio (sliders for 18 sensor values, 4 presets, XGBoost inference)
  • SHAP feature attribution chart, fault probability bars
  • Crew dispatch & reset actions (live API calls)
  • Maintenance work-order creation form
Other Pages & Components
  • /transformers/[id] — Asset detail: live prediction, sensor time-series charts, risk score
  • /weather/[district] — 30-day historical weather + 7-day forecast + crew pre-positioning plan for selected Gujarat district
  • GridMap.tsx — Leaflet map, pulsing radar markers coloured by risk level (CRITICAL=red, HIGH=orange, MEDIUM=yellow, LOW=green), animated 400kV/220kV power-line polylines, tile-style toggle (Dark SCADA / Highway Grid)
  • lib/api.ts — 22 exported async fetch functions covering all backend endpoints

10 Deployment Configuration

Local Development
  • Run src/setup.bat → creates venv, installs deps, copies .env, runs npm install
  • Run src/start.bat → launches FastAPI on :8000 and Next.js on :3000 in separate terminals
  • Database: Neon Serverless PostgreSQL (credentials in src/.env.example)
  • MapTiler key: CRFoY3RXgAloQLarTcRL (included for evaluation)
Vercel Production
  • vercel.json rewrites all /(.*) to /api/index.py
  • Root api/index.py adds src/backend to sys.path and imports app.main:app
  • APScheduler weekly retraining is disabled when VERCEL=1 env var is set
  • Tables auto-created at startup; exceptions on cold-start are gracefully warned

11 IBM Technology Integration

The submission declares three IBM integrations. These are planned/described in the README and submission.yaml but no IBM SDK code is present in the current source files — integration points are design-level references for the hackathon track.

07 Hard-Threshold Weather Risk Bucketing
08 Seeded Random — Synthetic Data Generation
09 Inverse Linear — Health-Index→Failure Prob
10 Manual Post-Calibration Overrides

01 · XGBoost Regressor — Failure Probability Estimation

CURRENT
XGBRegressor (reg:squarederror) — 150 trees, depth 5, lr 0.05
File: ml/train.py · ml_service.py | Task: continuous failure probability (0–1)
What it does well
  • Fast tabular inference (<1ms per sample)
  • Handles mixed feature scales without normalisation
  • Built-in feature importance via gain/split count
  • Tolerates missing values natively
Critical limitations
  • Output is a point estimate — no uncertainty band (says 0.74, but is it 0.60–0.88?)
  • Trained on 800 synthetic samples — tiny for a regression task
  • R² = 0.748 means ~25% of variance is unexplained
  • No temporal awareness: treats each reading as independent, ignores sensor drift over time
  • Post-hoc calibration overrides (C₂H₂ ≥ 20 → prob += rule) defeat what the model learned
Modern Replacement: Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT) or N-BEATS with Quantile Regression
A Temporal Fusion Transformer (Lim et al., 2021 — NeurIPS best paper) treats each transformer asset's sensor stream as a multi-variate time series. It outputs quantile prediction intervals (P10, P50, P90) — so instead of saying "failure probability = 0.74" it says "74% median, 90th-percentile window is 0.91", giving operators a calibrated confidence range. It handles multi-horizon forecasting (6h, 24h, 48h, 7d) as a single model output, eliminating the threshold bucketing step entirely. For smaller datasets, N-BEATS (Oreshkin et al., 2020) or Neural Prophet (a Facebook open-source model) provide strong uncertainty estimation with far fewer parameters.
ApproachUncertainty OutputTemporal AwarenessProduction Maturity
XGBoost (current)❌ None❌ None✅ Very high
Temporal Fusion Transformer✅ Quantile bands✅ Full sequence✅ PyTorch Forecasting
Gaussian Process Regression✅ Native Bayesian CI⚠️ Limited scale✅ GPyTorch
CatBoost + MAPIE conformal✅ Conformal intervals❌ Tabular only✅ Drop-in swap
XGBoost + MAPIE (easiest upgrade)✅ Conformal intervals❌ Tabular only✅ 2-line addition

Reference: Lim et al. (2021) "Temporal Fusion Transformers for Interpretable Multi-horizon Time Series Forecasting" — Int. J. Forecasting. Papadopoulos (2008) MAPIE conformal prediction.

02 · XGBoost Multi-class Classifier — Fault Mode Detection

CURRENT
XGBClassifier (multi:softprob) — 120 trees, depth 4, lr 0.08, 6 classes
File: ml/train.py:219–232 | Task: Arcing / Overheating / Dielectric / Mechanical / Insulation / Normal
What it does well
  • 98.75% accuracy on 800 samples (but those labels were algorithmically generated from the same rules)
  • softprob gives a probability distribution across all 6 classes
  • Very fast inference
Critical limitations
  • Label leakage: fault class labels were generated by the same if/elif thresholds the model learns, making 98.75% accuracy circular and not meaningful on real data
  • Class imbalance unaddressed — real grid failures are rare events (<2% of readings)
  • No ordinal awareness: Insulation Degradation → Arcing is a progression, but the model treats them as unrelated classes
  • DGA gases are highly correlated — multicollinearity inflates some feature importances
Modern Replacement 1 (Tabular): LightGBM + SMOTE-ENN for imbalanced classes
LightGBM with leaf-wise tree growth trains 2–5× faster than XGBoost on large imbalanced datasets and natively supports is_unbalance=True. Combined with SMOTE-ENN (synthetic minority oversampling + edited nearest-neighbours cleaning), the rare fault classes (Arcing, Dielectric Breakdown) get sufficient representation. The ordinal structure can be modelled with ordinal classification (Frank & Hall, 2001) wrapping LightGBM.
Modern Replacement 2 (Domain-specific): Graph Neural Network on transformer topology
Each transformer's DGA readings are correlated with upstream/downstream substation readings. A Graph Attention Network (GAT) treating the 836-asset Gujarat grid as a graph can propagate risk signals along transmission corridors. When Mundra's sensors degrade, a GAT model infers elevated risk at connected Kutch substations — something flat tabular XGBoost cannot express. Research: Deng et al. (2021) "Graph Convolutional Networks for Power System Fault Diagnosis" — IEEE Trans. Power Systems.
ApproachHandles ImbalanceGrid TopologyInterpretability
XGBoost (current)❌ Manual overrides❌ None✅ SHAP
LightGBM + SMOTE-ENN✅ Native❌ None✅ SHAP
TabNet (Arik & Pfister 2021)⚠️ Requires tuning❌ None✅ Attention masks
Graph Attention Network✅ Node-level weights✅ Full grid graph⚠️ GNNExplainer needed
Isolation Forest (anomaly)✅ Unsupervised❌ None⚠️ Limited

Reference: Ke et al. (2017) LightGBM: A Highly Efficient Gradient Boosting Decision Tree. Chawla et al. (2002) SMOTE. Arik & Pfister (2021) TabNet: Attentive Interpretable Tabular Learning.

03 · SHAP TreeExplainer — Feature Attribution

CURRENT
shap.TreeExplainer — local per-inference SHAP values
File: ml_service.py:157–189 | Role: top-5 feature drivers for each prediction
What it does well
  • Theoretically grounded (Shapley game theory)
  • TreeExplainer is O(TLD) — fast for trees
  • Both local (per-sample) and global explanations
  • Directional: positive = increased risk, negative = decreased
Limitations
  • SHAP creates a new TreeExplainer object on every request — severe performance penalty at scale
  • TreeSHAP assumes feature independence; DGA gases are correlated, violating this assumption
  • Falls back silently to static global importances when shap is not installed — gives wrong per-sample explanations
  • No causal explanation — SHAP correlation ≠ causation for grid operators
Modern Replacement: SHAP + Causal Shapley Values / CausalML
Causal Shapley Values (Heskes et al., 2020) extend SHAP to account for the known causal structure of DGA chemistry (C₂H₂ causes arcing, not the reverse). For a grid application where the causal DAG is known from IEC 60599, this produces operator-correct explanations: "acetylene rose because of the thermal event, not independently". Practically, dowhy + SHAP or econml integrations achieve this. For the immediate performance issue, the explainer should be cached at model-load time (not created per request), reducing explain latency from ~200ms to ~5ms.
Alternative: LIME with physics constraint injection
LIME (Ribeiro et al., 2016) fits a local linear model around each prediction. When domain constraints are injected (e.g., "C₂H₂/C₂H₄ ratio > 1 is diagnostic for arcing per IEC 60599") as LIME feature groups, the explanations are more domain-aligned than raw SHAP values for non-data-scientists (field engineers).

Reference: Heskes et al. (2020) "Causal Shapley Values: Exploiting Causal Knowledge to Explain Individual Predictions of Complex Models" — NeurIPS 2020. Ribeiro et al. (2016) LIME, KDD.

04 · IEC 60599 / Rogers Ratios — Rule-Based DGA Feature Engineering

CURRENT
Manual ratio features: CH₄/H₂, C₂H₄/C₂H₆, C₂H₂/C₂H₄ + hard threshold labels
File: train.py:111–150 | Role: DGA chemistry feature engineering and fault label assignment
What it does well
  • IEC 60599 Rogers Ratios are internationally standardised and validated on decades of real DGA data
  • Domain-informed features outperform raw gas concentrations alone
  • Transparent: human-readable fault assignment rules
Limitations
  • Rogers Ratios have known unclassifiable zone problem — ~30% of real DGA samples fall outside defined ratio boundaries
  • Hard threshold labels (C₂H₂ > 12 → Arcing) create a perfectly learnable rule, not a generalising model
  • Missing Duval Triangle method — considered superior to Rogers Ratios by IEC TC 10
  • Only 3 of 5 IEC 60599 key gas ratios are computed (missing C₂H₂/CH₄ = Key Ratio 5)
Modern Replacement: Duval Pentagon + Fuzzy Logic Membership
The Duval Triangle/Pentagon method (Michel Duval, IEEE, 2002) plots DGA ratios as ternary coordinates and uses convex polygon regions per fault mode. Unlike hard thresholds, it handles boundary cases by assigning partial membership — a reading at the Arcing/Overheating boundary gets 60% Arcing, 40% Overheating, which feeds more truthful soft labels into the ML model. The Pentagon extends coverage to Low-Energy Discharges (PD) and Stray Gassing, which Rogers misses. Implemented as a Python geometry check (shapely), this replaces the if/elif label chain with probabilistic soft labels for training.
Complementary: IEC 61869-based Dissolved Key Gas (DKG) method
The newer IEC 61869 standard introduces absolute gas-generation-rate features (ppm/day change per gas) instead of ratio snapshots. This captures whether a transformer is deteriorating rapidly vs. being at a stable elevated level — a critical distinction the current static features cannot make.

Reference: Duval, M. & dePabla, A. (2001) "Interpretation of Gas-in-Oil Analysis Using New IEC Publication 60599 and IEC TC 10 Databases" — IEEE Electrical Insulation Magazine. Shintemirov et al. (2009) IEEE Trans. Dielectrics.

05 · Linear Weighted Scoring — Composite Risk Score

CURRENT
overall_risk = 0.60 × failure_prob×100 + 0.30 × impact_score + 0.10 × weather_risk
File: scripts/ingest_risks.py:87–93 | Role: composite asset risk score (0–100)
What it does well
  • Transparent and explainable to operators
  • Fast to compute (arithmetic)
  • Weights reflect domain priority (probability first)
Limitations
  • Fixed weights (0.60 / 0.30 / 0.10) are arbitrary — never validated against actual outage outcomes
  • Linear additive model assumes independence between failure probability and weather risk — in reality they compound non-linearly (wet insulation + high load = exponentially higher risk)
  • Weather risk in the script is random.uniform(10, 80) seeded per asset ID — not real weather data
  • Impact-Adjusted Risk in dashboard.py uses a different formula (0.60 risk + 0.40 customer norm) creating inconsistency
Modern Replacement: AHP (Analytic Hierarchy Process) + Entropy Weighting
Analytic Hierarchy Process (Saaty, 1980) derives weights from pairwise expert comparisons: "Is failure probability 3× more important than customer impact for dispatch priority?" This produces empirically validated weights instead of hand-picked constants. Entropy Weighting (Shannon, 1948) automatically derives weights from the variance of each factor across assets — features with more discriminative power get higher weight. Combined as AHP-Entropy, this is widely used in power system risk studies (Chen et al., 2021 — IEEE TPWRS).
Alternative: Multi-Criteria Decision Making (MCDM) — TOPSIS or VIKOR
TOPSIS (Technique for Order of Preference by Similarity to Ideal Solution) ranks assets by their geometric distance from the "ideal best" (no risk, max customers served) and "ideal worst" (certain failure, most customers). This handles non-linear interactions between risk dimensions automatically. VIKOR additionally provides compromise solutions accounting for regret minimisation — critical for dispatcher decision making under time pressure. Both are parameter-free (no weight tuning) and produce ranked lists directly.

Reference: Saaty (1980) The Analytic Hierarchy Process. Hwang & Yoon (1981) Multiple Attribute Decision Making: Methods and Applications. Chen et al. (2021) "Transformer Risk Assessment" — IEEE TPWRS.

06 · Euclidean Distance — Crew Dispatch Proximity

CURRENT
math.hypot(Δlat, Δlon) × 111 km — nearest critical asset selection
File: api/crews.py:60–63, 71 | Role: select closest critical asset for crew dispatch + ETA
What it does well
  • O(n) scan — trivially fast for 12 crews × 836 assets
  • Easy to reason about
  • Handles null asset_id gracefully
Critical limitations
  • Euclidean distance is wrong for geographical coordinates — error up to 11% at Gujarat's latitude range (20°–25°N)
  • Straight-line distance ignores roads, terrain, and Gujarat's river crossings (Narmada, Tapi, Sabarmati)
  • ETA formula (dist × 2.2 mins/km) is a flat constant — ignores rush hour, monsoon road conditions, highway vs. village roads
  • Single-criterion greedy selection: dispatch the nearest crew to the nearest critical asset. Ignores crew specialization mismatch (a substation electrician dispatched to a transformer DGA crisis)
  • No multi-crew coordination: if 3 critical assets are near each other, the same crew could be sent to all 3 sequentially
Modern Replacement 1: Haversine + OSRM Routing + Hungarian Algorithm
Replace math.hypot with Haversine formula (correct for sphere geometry). Replace the flat ETA constant with the OSRM (Open Source Routing Machine) API or Valhalla routing engine — both are free and self-hostable — to get real road-network travel times. For the multi-crew multi-incident assignment problem, use the Hungarian Algorithm (Kuhn, 1955) or its modern variant Jonker-Volgenant from scipy.optimize.linear_sum_assignment to find the globally optimal crew-to-incident assignment matrix (minimising total travel time while maximising skill match score).
Modern Replacement 2: Vehicle Routing Problem (VRP) with time windows
When multiple crews and multiple incidents exist simultaneously, the dispatch problem is a Capacitated VRP with Time Windows (CVRPTW). Google OR-Tools solves this exactly for 12 crews and ~50 critical assets in milliseconds. Each crew's skill set (transformer DGA specialist, substation engineer, cable fault locator) becomes a capacity constraint. Each incident's urgency (6h vs 24h window) becomes the time window. This transforms dispatch from greedy nearest-first to a globally optimal assignment guaranteed to minimise total outage time.
ApproachDistance AccuracyRoad-AwareMulti-Crew Optimal
Euclidean (current)❌ ~11% error❌ No❌ Greedy
Haversine✅ Correct❌ No❌ Greedy
OSRM + Haversine✅ Correct✅ Yes❌ Greedy
Hungarian + OSRM✅ Correct✅ Yes✅ Global optimum
OR-Tools CVRPTW✅ Correct✅ Yes✅ Global + time windows

Reference: Kuhn (1955) "The Hungarian Method for the Assignment Problem" — Naval Research Logistics Quarterly. Google OR-Tools VRP documentation (2023). OSRM project (openstreetmap.org).

07 · Hard-Threshold Weather Risk Bucketing

CURRENT
if wind > 60 → HIGH; elif wind > 30 or rain > 20 → MEDIUM; else LOW
Files: api/weather.py:68–74, weather.py:209–213, weather.py:295–300 | Role: weather risk classification
What it does well
  • Operationally clear — operators understand "HIGH" immediately
  • Zero computation cost
  • Matches rough IMD (India Meteorological Dept.) warning thresholds
Limitations
  • Binary step function: 59 km/h wind = LOW, 61 km/h = HIGH — discontinuous and unrealistic
  • Temperature is ignored entirely — 47°C heatwave (Gujarat summer) causes oil temperature rise and load spikes, but gets "LOW" weather risk
  • Humidity ignored — wet insulation + any wind = conductor flashover risk
  • Interaction effects ignored: 25 mm rain + 35 km/h wind together exceed either individual threshold
  • History/forecast endpoints use seeded-random sinusoidal data, not actual weather models
Modern Replacement: Multi-variate Fuzzy Inference System (FIS) for Weather Risk
A Mamdani Fuzzy Inference System replaces hard thresholds with overlapping membership functions: wind speed transitions smoothly from LOW to MEDIUM to HIGH across a continuous range. More importantly, a fuzzy system handles the compound interaction: IF wind IS medium AND humidity IS high AND temp IS very_high THEN risk IS high. This matches how experienced grid operators actually assess weather risk. Libraries: scikit-fuzzy (Python, MIT license).
Alternative: NWP-integrated Risk Index (ERA5 + ECMWF API)
Replace OpenWeatherMap's current-conditions-only API with the ECMWF ERA5 reanalysis dataset (free, global, 31-km resolution) for historical weather, and the ECMWF Open API for 10-day ensemble forecasts with uncertainty bands. For Gujarat-specific grid risk, the IMD API (India Meteorological Department) provides official cyclone, thunderstorm, and heatwave alerts that map directly to grid threat categories. Combined, this gives both a historical baseline and probabilistic future risk — replacing the current seeded-random sinusoidal history generator.

Reference: Zadeh (1965) "Fuzzy Sets." Hersbach et al. (2020) "The ERA5 global reanalysis" — Quarterly Journal of the Royal Meteorological Society.

08 · Seeded-Random Synthetic Data Generation

CURRENT
numpy.random.uniform / betavariate with manual risk scoring formulas
Files: train.py:65–178, expand_gujarat_grid.py:160–186 | Role: training data + risk seed generation
What it does well
  • Produces enough volume (800 samples) to train a tree model
  • Gujarat monsoon patterns encoded in wind/rainfall distribution weights
  • Beta distribution (α=2, β=3) for risk scores is more realistic than pure uniform
Limitations
  • The DGA gas values are statistically independent uniform draws — in reality, H₂, CH₄, C₂H₄ are physically correlated (they share pyrolysis pathways)
  • 800 training samples is below the minimum recommended for a 22-feature model (rule of thumb: 10–30 samples/feature = 220–660 minimum)
  • Fault labels generated by the same thresholds as the label-assignment code creates perfect circular learning
  • Weather and DGA features are generated independently when real-world compounding effects exist (monsoon moisture accelerates insulation degradation)
Modern Replacement: Conditional Tabular GAN (CTGAN) or TVAE
CTGAN (Xu et al., NeurIPS 2019) is specifically designed for synthetic tabular data with mixed feature distributions (continuous DGA gases + categorical fault modes). It learns the joint distribution of all 22 features including inter-gas correlations from a small real dataset (even 200–300 real DGA rows are sufficient as a seed), then generates thousands of realistic samples. The sdv (Synthetic Data Vault) Python library provides CTGAN, TVAE, and CopulaGAN in 5 lines. Crucially, CTGAN preserves the covariance structure of real DGA chemistry that uniform random sampling destroys.
Open Dataset Alternative: IEEE PES DGA Public Datasets
The IEEE PES Task Force on DGA has published open transformer DGA datasets (CIGRE, IEC TC 10 databases). The UCI Machine Learning Repository hosts the "Electrical Fault Detection" dataset. Using real DGA data — even augmented with CTGAN — produces a model with genuine generalization capability, unlike the current purely synthetic pipeline.

Reference: Xu et al. (2019) "Modeling Tabular Data using Conditional GAN" — NeurIPS 2019. CIGRE WG A2.49 (2019) "Condition Assessment of Power Transformers."

09 · Inverse Linear Transform — Health Index → Failure Probability

CURRENT
failure_prob = (100 − health_index) / 100  |  health_score = (1 − prob) × 100
Files: ingest_predictions.py:49–54, ml_service.py:134 | Role: bidirectional HI↔probability conversion
What it does well
  • Simple bijection: easy to communicate to operators
  • Always in [0,1] range
  • Health=0 → prob=1.0, Health=100 → prob=0.0 (semantically correct)
Limitations
  • Assumes a perfectly linear relationship between health degradation and failure probability — this is physically wrong. Failure probability is non-linear: a transformer at Health=30 is far more than 70% likely to fail soon, not exactly 70%
  • The Weibull distribution is the industry standard for transformer failure probability — linear inversion ignores aging kinetics
  • Circular: health_score in ml_service is computed from predicted failure_prob, which is then stored as health_score in the Prediction table, which is later used to derive failure_prob — a loop
Modern Replacement: Weibull Proportional Hazard Model
The Weibull distribution (shape parameter β, scale parameter η) is the IEEE C57.91-validated standard for transformer aging and failure probability. The survival function S(t) = exp(−(t/η)^β) gives cumulative failure probability as a function of asset age and stress indicators. A Cox Proportional Hazards Model extends this to include time-varying covariates (DGA gas levels, load percentage) as multiplicative risk modifiers. Libraries: lifelines (Python). This replaces the linear inversion with a physically grounded survival analysis that accounts for transformer aging kinetics and the bathtub failure-rate curve.

Reference: IEEE C57.91-2011 "Guide for Loading Mineral-Oil-Immersed Transformers." Cox (1972) "Regression Models and Life-Tables." Davidson-Pilon (2019) Lifelines documentation.

10 · Manual Post-Calibration Overrides

CURRENT
if c2h2 ≥ 20 → prob = max(prob, 0.82 + …); if oil_temp ≥ 90 → prob = max(prob, 0.84 + …)
File: ml_service.py:116–129 | Role: hard-coded physical safety overrides after XGBoost inference
What it does well
  • Encodes known physical safety rules (C₂H₂ above 20 ppm is universally critical per IEC 60599)
  • Prevents ML model from under-predicting at known dangerous thresholds
  • Fast: pure arithmetic
Limitations
  • This is an admission the ML model is unreliable at critical ranges — a model requiring post-hoc correction was undertrained
  • Arbitrary formulas: 0.82 + (c2h2 − 20) × 0.005 is not derived from any standard
  • Creates a non-differentiable, non-monotonic probability surface — can cause the risk level to jump between requests if sensor readings oscillate around a threshold
  • Four separate independent override conditions may conflict or double-count risk
Modern Replacement: Isotonic Regression Calibration + Constraint-Aware Training
Instead of post-hoc overrides, the correct approach is Platt scaling or isotonic regression calibration (sklearn CalibratedClassifierCV) which learns the correct probability mapping from a calibration set. For the critical regions specifically, training with monotonic constraints (XGBoost natively supports monotone_constraints) ensures the model predicts higher failure probability as C₂H₂ increases, eliminating the need for any override. Bounded ISOTONIC calibration additionally enforces that prob stays in [0,1] and increases monotonically with each risk factor — a formal guarantee the current overrides try (and fail) to approximate.

Reference: Platt (1999) "Probabilistic Outputs for Support Vector Machines." Niculescu-Mizil & Caruana (2005) "Predicting Good Probabilities with Supervised Learning" — ICML.

11 · 80/20 Random Holdout Split — Model Validation

CURRENT
train_test_split(test_size=0.20, random_state=42)
File: train.py:191–193 | Role: evaluation of both regressor and classifier
What it does well
  • Standard, reproducible (random_state=42)
  • Simple to implement and understand
  • 160 test samples provides some statistical power
Limitations
  • 800 samples with 22 features and a 20% split gives only 160 test samples — 95% CI for accuracy at 98.75% is ±1.7% which is non-trivial
  • Random split on synthetic data where train and test have identical distributions gives optimistically biased accuracy
  • For time-series sensor data (where future readings of a sensor depend on past ones), random splitting causes data leakage — temporal splits are required
  • Single split — high variance estimate. 5-fold CV would give much more stable metric estimates
Modern Replacement: Time-Series Nested Cross-Validation with Walk-Forward
For sequential sensor data, TimeSeriesSplit (sklearn) performs walk-forward validation: train on months 1–6, test on month 7; train on months 1–7, test on month 8; etc. This is the correct protocol for systems where the future must not inform the past. Combined with nested cross-validation (inner CV for hyperparameter tuning, outer CV for unbiased accuracy estimation), this produces a statistically honest performance estimate. For the current synthetic tabular case, Stratified K-Fold (k=10) across all 6 fault classes ensures each fold contains proportional representation of rare classes.
Additional: Calibration Curves and Brier Score for probability outputs
For a regression model outputting failure probability, RMSE and R² alone are insufficient. Reliability diagrams (calibration curves) and the Brier Score verify that "when the model says 0.80 probability, failures actually occur ~80% of the time." The current model has no calibration evaluation at all.

Reference: Kohavi (1995) "A Study of Cross-Validation and Bootstrap for Accuracy Estimation" — IJCAI. Bergstra & Bengio (2012) "Random Search for Hyper-Parameter Optimization" — JMLR.

12 · Weekly Cron Retraining — APScheduler

CURRENT
scheduler.add_job(train, 'cron', day_of_week='sun', hour=0)
File: app/main.py:35 | Role: automated weekly ML model retraining
What it does well
  • Ensures model is periodically updated with new sensor data
  • Disabled on Vercel (prevents serverless timeout issues)
  • No infrastructure dependency (runs in-process)
Limitations
  • Calendar-based retraining ignores data drift — the model retrained every Sunday regardless of whether sensor distributions have changed at all
  • No statistical trigger: if a new type of fault appears in week 3 (e.g., monsoon-induced corrosion), the model waits until Sunday to learn it
  • Full retraining on 800 samples each time — no incremental learning, no memory of previous model performance
  • No champion/challenger framework: the new model automatically replaces the old one without A/B testing
  • MLflow is used but model promotion is not gated on performance thresholds
Modern Replacement: Evidently AI Drift Detection + Triggered Retraining
Evidently AI or NannyML monitors incoming sensor telemetry for data drift (distribution shift in DGA gas values) and model performance drift (when predictions diverge from actuals) using Population Stability Index (PSI) and Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) tests. Retraining is triggered only when drift is statistically detected (p < 0.05), not on an arbitrary calendar. Combined with MLflow Model Registry stage promotion (Staging → Production requires passing accuracy threshold + drift checks), this creates a production-grade ML lifecycle with guardrails. River (Python online ML library) additionally enables incremental/online learning from each new sensor batch without full retraining.
StrategyDrift-AwareIncrementalChampion/Challenger
Weekly cron (current)❌ Calendar only❌ Full retrain❌ None
Evidently + triggered retrain✅ PSI/MMD tests❌ Full retrain✅ MLflow gates
River online learning✅ Continuous✅ Per-sample update⚠️ Limited
Evidently + River hybrid✅ Both✅ Online + triggered✅ Full lifecycle

Reference: Gama et al. (2014) "A Survey on Concept Drift Adaptation" — ACM Computing Surveys. Montiel et al. (2021) "River: machine learning for streaming data in Python." NannyML documentation (2023).

01 · XGBoost Regressor — Failure Probability Estimation

CURRENT
XGBRegressor (reg:squarederror) — 150 trees, depth 5, lr 0.05
File: ml/train.py · ml_service.py | Task: continuous failure probability (0–1)
What it does well
  • Fast tabular inference (<1ms per sample)
  • Handles mixed feature scales without normalisation
  • Built-in feature importance via gain/split count
  • Tolerates missing values natively
Critical limitations
  • Output is a point estimate — no uncertainty band (says 0.74, but is it 0.60–0.88?)
  • Trained on 800 synthetic samples — tiny for a regression task
  • R² = 0.748 means ~25% of variance is unexplained
  • No temporal awareness: treats each reading as independent, ignores sensor drift over time
  • Post-hoc calibration overrides (C₂H₂ ≥ 20 → prob += rule) defeat what the model learned
Modern Replacement: Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT) or N-BEATS with Quantile Regression
A Temporal Fusion Transformer (Lim et al., 2021 — NeurIPS best paper) treats each transformer asset's sensor stream as a multi-variate time series. It outputs quantile prediction intervals (P10, P50, P90) — so instead of saying "failure probability = 0.74" it says "74% median, 90th-percentile window is 0.91", giving operators a calibrated confidence range. It handles multi-horizon forecasting (6h, 24h, 48h, 7d) as a single model output, eliminating the threshold bucketing step entirely. For smaller datasets, N-BEATS (Oreshkin et al., 2020) or Neural Prophet (a Facebook open-source model) provide strong uncertainty estimation with far fewer parameters.
